For a plain page, the page-design guidance follows. It is the `artifact-design` skill's own text, so do not load that skill as well. Write the page to a file and publish it in the same message: the two calls run in order.

## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

args.content:
---
name: baton
description: Move AI work between tools without losing it. Imports a ChatGPT share link, a ChatGPT or Claude data export, or a Claude Code session log into an audited handoff bundle (HANDOFF.md, the full transcript with reasoning and tool calls, recovered files and a loss audit), then continues the work. It can also export the current session as a handoff for another agent or teammate, or for Jira, Salesforce, Zendesk or Slack. Use when the user pastes a chatgpt.com/share link, asks to continue work started in ChatGPT, Claude or another assistant, asks to hand off, export or package this session, or asks what was lost when moving a conversation.
---

# Baton: hand off AI work, not just chat text

Baton turns a conversation into a **bundle**: a folder an agent or a person can pick up and continue.

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `HANDOFF.md` | **Start here.** Goal, every user prompt verbatim, where it stopped, open threads, reasoning trail, file status, losses |
| `PROMPT.md` | One paste-ready block for chat apps that cannot read folders |
| `TRANSCRIPT.md` | Full chronological record. Reasoning, tool calls and outputs are folded. |
| `LOSS_AUDIT.md` | What the source did **not** include (redacted tool outputs, blank code, undownloadable files) |
| `files/` | Files rebuilt from the code that created them, each **recovered**, **stale** or **lost** |
| `replay/` | The source's code cells, to regenerate PDFs, ZIPs and similar outputs in a sandbox (never run automatically) |
| `bundle.json` | Canonical machine-readable record with a SHA-256 hash chain |
| `SKILL.md` / `AGENTS.md` | Make the bundle itself a "continue this work" skill / agent context |

## Running it

The CLI ships inside this skill. In the commands below, `BATON` means
`node <this skill's base directory>/scripts/baton.mjs` (Node 18 or newer, no install needed).

## Import and continue (the common case)

1. Run the import. The source can be a share URL, a saved `.html` page, an export `.zip` / `conversations.json`, or a `.jsonl` session:
   ```bash
   BATON import "<source>" -o handoffs/<short-name>
   ```
   Add `--pick "<title words>"` for account exports with many conversations.
2. Read `handoffs/<short-name>/HANDOFF.md` in full. Open `TRANSCRIPT.md` only for the turns you need (search it with Grep).
3. Tell the user in 3–5 lines: the goal, where the work stopped, how many files were recovered, stale or lost, and the high-severity losses.
   **Never claim a lost file exists.**
4. Ask whether to continue from the latest instruction. If yes, copy `files/` into the workspace and carry on.
   Rebuild **lost** files from their descriptions in the transcript, and check **stale** files before relying on them.
5. When a chunk of work is done, write `handoffs/<short-name>/STATE.md` (goal, decisions, next steps).

If fetching a share URL fails (login wall, rate limit, or a private link), ask the user to open the link, save the page as
"Webpage, HTML only", and give you the file path.

## Hand off this session

```bash
BATON session latest -o handoffs/<short-name>            # this project's newest Claude Code session
BATON session latest -o handoffs/<short-name> --zip      # also a .zip to send to someone
BATON session latest --install-skill                     # also install as .claude/skills/continue-<title>/
```
Then show the user `HANDOFF.md` §3–§7 and the bundle path. Mention `PROMPT.md` for pasting into another chat app.

## File it in a business system

```bash
BATON sink handoffs/<name> --to jira --jira-project OPS        # prints the payload (dry run)
BATON sink handoffs/<name> --to salesforce --post              # sends it; needs SALESFORCE_INSTANCE_URL + SALESFORCE_ACCESS_TOKEN
```
Systems: `salesforce` (Case + note + tasks, or `--sf-parent <recordId>`), `jira` (issue in Atlassian Document Format),
`zendesk` (internal-note ticket), `slack` (Block Kit to `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`). **Only use `--post` when the user asks you to send it.**

## Check and inspect

```bash
BATON inspect "<source>"        # dry run: what would transfer, what would not
BATON verify handoffs/<name>    # recompute the hash chain; exit 2 if anything was edited
```

## Rules

- Secrets and personal data are redacted by default. Use `--no-redact` only if the user explicitly asks.
- Private context (system prompts, memory, harness notes) is excluded unless `--include-hidden` is passed.
- Never run `replay/` cells without the user's approval. They are third-party code from another AI's sandbox.
- Fetch only the URL the user gave you, one page per request.

args.content:
# Baton bundle format: `baton.bundle/v1`

**Status:** draft 1 (2026-10-11) · **License:** CC-BY-4.0 for this document, Apache-2.0 for the reference implementation

A Baton bundle is a vendor-neutral record of a piece of AI work: what the user asked, what the assistant
said and reasoned, which tools it ran, which files it produced, and **what the source failed to include**.
A bundle is designed to be read by three audiences at once: an AI agent continuing the work, a person reviewing it, and a
system of record filing it.

## 1. Layout

A bundle is a directory (or a ZIP of one). Only `bundle.json` is normative. Everything else is a rendering of it.

```
<slug>/
  bundle.json      REQUIRED  canonical record (this spec)
  HANDOFF.md       RECOMMENDED  agent + human brief; front matter repeats id, source and root_hash
  PROMPT.md        paste-ready single block for chat UIs
  TRANSCRIPT.md    chronological rendering
  LOSS_AUDIT.md    rendering of `loss` + `artifacts`
  index.html       offline viewer (must not load remote resources)
  SKILL.md         Agent Skills front matter (`name`, `description`) so the folder is a skill
  AGENTS.md        pointer for agents that read AGENTS.md
  files/<path>     artifact contents for status recovered | stale | attached
  replay/          optional: source code cells + a sandboxed runner
  sinks/<system>.json  optional: business-system payloads
  source/          optional: the raw input
```

## 2. `bundle.json`

```ts
interface BatonBundle {
  schema: 'baton.bundle/v1';
  id: string;                 // 16 hex chars, sha256(kind ␀ conversationId|url ␀ title ␀ firstEventText)[:16]
  title: string;
  source: {
    kind: 'chatgpt-share' | 'chatgpt-export' | 'claude-export' | 'claude-code' | 'openai-messages' | 'unknown';
    tool: string;             // human name of the source product
    url?: string; conversationId?: string; createdAt?: string; updatedAt?: string;
    model?: string; cwd?: string; gitBranch?: string;
  };
  events: BatonEvent[];       // chronological, the active branch only
  artifacts: BatonArtifact[]; // sorted by path
  loss: LossItem[];           // sorted by severity: high, warn, info
  links: string[];            // URLs referenced by messages or listed by the source
  redaction: { enabled: boolean; counts: Record<string, number> };
  integrity: { algorithm: 'sha256-chain'; root: string; count: number };
  stats: BundleStats;
  generator: { name: string; version: string; generatedAt: string };
}
```

### 2.1 Events

| `kind` | `role` | `text` | Other fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| `message` | user / assistant | Markdown | `hidden` = progress update hidden in the source UI |
| `reasoning` | assistant | reasoning text or summary | `meta.granularity` = `summary` \| `full`. `redactedBySource` when only a signature or ciphertext exists. |
| `tool_call` | assistant | short label | `tool.{name,title,language,input,args,callId}`. `redactedBySource` when the input is missing. |
| `tool_result` | tool | output | `tool.name`, `tool.callId`. `redactedBySource` when the source shows a placeholder. |
| `attachment` | user | description | `meta.{name,size,mimeType}` |
| `note` | any | structural marker | `meta.private = true` for private context (excluded by default) |

`tool.args` carries structured arguments only for file-editing tools (`Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`),
because artifact recovery replays them.

### 2.2 Artifacts

| `status` | Meaning | `content` |
|---|---|---|
| `recovered` | reconstructed byte for byte from the code or tool call that wrote it | present |
| `stale` | the last full write was recovered, but later modifications could not be replayed statically | present |
| `lost` | created or linked by the conversation, but its content is not in the source | absent |
| `attached` | content shipped with the source (for example, text extracted from an upload) | present |

`sha256` is the hex digest of the UTF-8 content. `recoveredFrom` / `modifiedBy` list event ids. `note` explains the status.
Paths are POSIX, relative and normalised. Absolute paths outside the source's working root are prefixed `_abs/`.
Paths never contain `..`.

### 2.3 Loss items

`{category, count, severity: 'high'|'warn'|'info', detail}`. Categories in v1: `tool-outputs`, `tool-inputs`,
`files-lost`, `files-stale`, `files-recovered`, `citations`, `images`, `user-attachments`, `branches`,
`reasoning-depth`, `memory`, `harness-context`, `subagents`, `private-context`, `baton-redactions`, `unreadable-lines`.
Producers may add categories. Consumers must display unknown ones verbatim.

## 3. Integrity

```
h0 = sha256("baton.bundle/v1")
hi = sha256(h(i-1) || stableJSON(event_i without "hash"))    for each event, in order; event_i.hash = hi
then, for each artifact sorted by path:
h  = sha256(h || stableJSON({path, status, sha256}))
root = h
```

`stableJSON` is JSON with object keys sorted lexicographically, `undefined` members dropped, and no whitespace.
A verifier recomputes artifact digests from `files/<path>` when present (otherwise from embedded `content`) and compares
the root. This gives **tamper-evidence** only. Anchoring the root externally (for example in WORM storage or a transparency log)
is out of scope for v1.

## 4. Privacy requirements for producers

1. Redaction of secrets and personal data **on by default**, with counts recorded in `redaction.counts`.
2. Private context (system prompts, memory, custom instructions, harness metadata) **excluded by default** and counted in `loss`.
3. Replay code is never executed by the producer.
4. Network access is limited to the single URL the user supplied.

## 5. Versioning

Additive fields do not change the schema id. A breaking change bumps it to `baton.bundle/v2`. Consumers should
ignore unknown fields and reject unknown major versions.

args.content:
# Baton

**Hand off AI work, not just chat text.**

Baton turns an AI conversation into a **handoff bundle** that another tool, agent, teammate or business system can pick up and continue.
Sources are a ChatGPT share link, a ChatGPT or Claude data export, or a Claude Code session. Each bundle carries:

- every prompt, verbatim
- the assistant's replies and reasoning
- every tool call and the code it ran
- the **files the session created, rebuilt from that code**
- a **loss audit** of everything the source failed to hand over
- a SHA-256 hash chain so any later edit is detectable

It runs locally with zero runtime dependencies and is free to use.

```
$ npx github:nimb-ou/App import https://chatgpt.com/share/6acbc222-2500-83ee-b38c-dcfe2b46e388
✓ Cricket Stumping Simulation
  source   ChatGPT (chatgpt-share) https://chatgpt.com/share/6acbc222-2500-83ee-b38c-dcfe2b46e388
  content  8 prompts · 20 replies · 47 reasoning · 133 tool calls
  files    13 recovered · 3 stale · 16 lost
  loss     163 tool-outputs · 81 tool-inputs · 16 files-lost (see LOSS_AUDIT.md)
  root     0e489b3a871206841699f7195e270a7198f60bca19e2defbb98ffb0ec416bac6
  → handoffs/cricket-stumping-simulation/HANDOFF.md  (start here)
```

That is a real public share link. Its page *looks* complete and says "Download the complete ZIP", but the share
silently drops all 163 tool outputs, 33 code cells and every generated file. Baton reports that, rebuilds **13 project files byte
for byte** from the code that wrote them, and lists the 16 it cannot recover (including `app.py`) instead of pretending they exist.
See [`examples/cricket-stumping/`](examples/cricket-stumping/) and its [`HANDOFF.md`](examples/cricket-stumping/HANDOFF.md).

## Why

AI work is stuck where it happened. Claude and Gemini both shipped "import memory" in March 2026, but that moves a **profile
of you**, not **the work**: the plan, decisions, code and files. Exporter extensions produce documents for humans. None
of them says what was lost, and none recovers files. The full analysis is in [`docs/research/01-market-landscape.md`](docs/research/01-market-landscape.md).

## Use it the way you work

| You are… | Use | How |
|---|---|---|
| In a terminal | **CLI** | `npx github:nimb-ou/App import <url-or-file>` (Node ≥ 18) |
| In Claude Code | **Plugin** (skill + `/baton:import`, `/baton:handoff` + MCP) | `/plugin marketplace add nimb-ou/App` then `/plugin install baton@baton` |
| In any Skills-aware agent (Codex, Cursor, …) | **Agent Skill** | copy [`skills/baton/`](skills/baton/) into the agent's skills folder. The CLI is bundled inside it. |
| In an MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, …) | **MCP server** | `{"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "github:nimb-ou/App", "mcp"]}` |
| In a browser | **Web app** | open [`web/dist/baton.html`](web/dist/baton.html) (one file, works offline) and drop a file. Nothing is uploaded. |
| In a team / company | **Sinks** | `baton sink <bundle> --to salesforce\|jira\|zendesk\|slack [--post]` |

### Sources

| Input | What it is |
|---|---|
| `https://chatgpt.com/share/<id>` | public ChatGPT share link: fetched once, no login |
| `share.html` | a share page saved from the browser (works when fetching is blocked) |
| `export.zip` / `conversations.json` | ChatGPT **or** Claude account data export (`--pick "<title>"` for one conversation) |
| `*.jsonl` / a directory | Claude Code session log (`baton session latest` finds this project's newest) |
| `messages.json` | any `[{role, content}]` log (OpenAI/Anthropic API style) |

### What a bundle contains

| File | For |
|---|---|
| `HANDOFF.md` | **Start here.** Goal · every prompt verbatim · where it stopped · open threads · reasoning trail · file status · losses · how to continue |
| `PROMPT.md` | one paste-ready block for ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or any chat that cannot read folders |
| `TRANSCRIPT.md` | everything, in order. Reasoning, tool calls and outputs are folded into `<details>`. |
| `LOSS_AUDIT.md` | what did not transfer, per-file status, integrity root |
| `files/` | rebuilt files: **recovered** (exact), **stale** (exact up to a later unreplayable edit), **lost** (listed, not faked) |
| `replay/` | the source's code cells plus a no-network Docker runner, to regenerate PDFs, ZIPs and similar outputs. Never run automatically. |
| `SKILL.md` · `AGENTS.md` | make the folder itself a "continue this work" skill or agent context |
| `index.html` | offline viewer with search |
| `bundle.json` | the canonical record: [`docs/SPEC.md`](docs/SPEC.md) |
| `sinks/*.json` | optional Salesforce / Jira / Zendesk / Slack payloads |

## CLI

```
baton import <source> [-o dir] [--zip] [--pick text] [--sink jira,slack] [--install-skill] [--no-redact] [--include-hidden]
baton session [latest|<id>]      bundle a Claude Code session from this project
baton inspect <source>           dry run: what would transfer, what would not
baton verify <bundle|zip>        recompute the hash chain (exit 2 if anything was edited)
baton sink <bundle> --to <system> [--post] [--jira-project KEY] [--sf-parent RECORD_ID]
baton mcp                        MCP server over stdio
```

Posting uses environment variables only: `SALESFORCE_INSTANCE_URL`/`SALESFORCE_ACCESS_TOKEN`,
`JIRA_BASE_URL`/`JIRA_EMAIL`/`JIRA_API_TOKEN`/`JIRA_PROJECT`, `ZENDESK_SUBDOMAIN`/`ZENDESK_EMAIL`/`ZENDESK_API_TOKEN`, `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`.

## Privacy and safety defaults

- **Local-first.** The CLI, skill and MCP server run on your machine. The web app parses in your browser.
- **Redaction on:** API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, AWS, Google, Slack, Stripe), JWTs, bearer tokens, private keys, passwords in
  assignments, emails, phone numbers and Luhn-valid card numbers. Turn off with `--no-redact`.
- **Private context off:** system prompts, memory, custom instructions and harness reminders are excluded (and counted) unless `--include-hidden` is set.
- **One URL, once:** only the public share link you pass is fetched. There is no crawling and no authentication.
- **No code execution:** replay cells are written, never run. Output paths are sanitised and writes outside the target directory are refused.

## How it is built

TypeScript with no runtime dependencies. Node ≥ 22.18 runs the source directly, and `dist/baton.mjs` is a single-file build for Node ≥ 18.

```
src/core       schema, turbo-stream decoder, SHA-256, ZIP, redaction, hash chain, build pipeline
src/parsers    ChatGPT (share + export), Claude export, Claude Code JSONL, generic logs, format detection
src/recover    file recovery (heredocs, Write/Edit replay, modification tracking) + replay kit
src/render     HANDOFF / PROMPT / TRANSCRIPT / LOSS_AUDIT / SKILL / AGENTS / index.html (safe Markdown)
src/sinks      Salesforce composite, Jira ADF, Zendesk, Slack Block Kit
src/mcp        JSON-RPC stdio server
src/node       fetch, file and zip IO, session discovery, posting
web/           client-side app (built to web/dist/baton.html)
```

```bash
npm install            # dev only: typescript, esbuild, @types/node
npm test               # 64 tests, incl. end-to-end on the real share fixture
npm run typecheck
npm run build          # dist/baton.mjs, skills/baton/scripts/baton.mjs, web/dist/*.html
npm run examples       # regenerate examples/ deterministically
```

## Business model (free to the user)

The person moving their work never pays. Revenue comes from whoever **gains** when work moves:
the receiving AI vendor (verified-migration "switching bounty"), employers (an **AI Work Record** layer that files
conversations into Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira or Zendesk with redaction, retention and integrity), and platforms that want an "Import from anywhere"
button. Data is never sold. Details are in [`docs/research/04-monetization.md`](docs/research/04-monetization.md) and [`05-business-layer.md`](docs/research/05-business-layer.md).

## Project record

This repo documents its own making. Every prompt, decision and result is kept:

- [`docs/prompts/`](docs/prompts/): the user's prompts, verbatim, with how each was interpreted
- [`docs/journal/`](docs/journal/): timestamped build journal (what was done, bugs found, results)
- [`docs/decisions/`](docs/decisions/): architecture decision records
- [`docs/research/`](docs/research/): market, formats, legal/policy, monetisation, business layer, loss findings (with sources)
- [`examples/this-build-session/`](examples/this-build-session/): **the Claude Code session that built Baton, exported by Baton**

## Roadmap

Browser extension for logged-in chats (same core) · Gemini Takeout parser · Cursor/Codex logs · statically replaying
Python `str.replace` patches · OAuth-managed connectors and retention policies for the business tier · external anchoring of
integrity roots · submitting the bundle format to the Data Transfer Initiative.

License: Apache-2.0. Format spec: CC-BY-4.0.

# Journal 03: Surfaces, tests, web app, packaging

**Window:** 2026-10-11 17:50 to 18:15 UTC

## Built

| Surface | Where | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| CLI (`import`, `session`, `inspect`, `verify`, `sink`, `mcp`) | `src/cli.ts`, `src/bin.ts`, `dist/baton.mjs` | e2e tests, live fetch of the real share URL (3 s, same root hash as the saved fixture) |
| MCP server (6 tools, JSON-RPC stdio, no SDK) | `src/mcp/server.ts` | scripted stdio session + unit tests (initialize, tools/list, tools/call, errors) |
| Business sinks (Salesforce composite, Jira ADF, Zendesk, Slack Block Kit) | `src/sinks/index.ts`, `src/node/post.ts` | payload-shape tests. Live posting not exercised (no credentials in this environment). |
| Agent Skill with the CLI bundled inside | `skills/baton/` | runs with plain `node`, no install |
| Claude Code plugin + marketplace + MCP config + 2 commands | `.claude-plugin/`, `.mcp.json`, `commands/` | `claude plugin validate`: passed |
| Web app, client-side only | `web/` → `web/dist/baton.html` | headless Chromium: example converts in about 130–200 ms, no console errors, no horizontal scroll at 400 px, light and dark |
| Live hosted copy of the web app | claude.ai Artifact (private to the owner), `downloads` capability for the .zip | published |
| Open format spec | `docs/SPEC.md` | n/a |
| CI | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (typecheck, tests, build drift, bundled-CLI smoke test) | runs on push |

## Test results

64 tests, 64 pass (see `docs/outputs/test-run.txt`). TypeScript strict mode reports 0 errors.

Tests that caught real bugs before shipping:
1. **Phone redaction inside UUIDs.** `7907aff6-3500-4321-9387-…` was redacted as a phone number. Fixed with identifier-aware boundaries.
2. **Card vs phone ordering.** A Luhn-valid card number was labelled PHONE. The card rule now runs first.
3. **Decimal digits as a card.** `0.014641999965533614` was redacted. Fixed with a `(?<![\w.-])` boundary.
4. **`/repo/../x` mapping.** It resolved to `x` inside the repo instead of `_abs/x`. Fixed by normalising dots before the prefix check.
5. **Tamper detection root.** Verify flagged altered files but recomputed the *recorded* digest, so the root matched. It now hashes the shipped bytes.
6. **Duplicate shebang** in the esbuild output (source shebang plus banner). Removed the banner.

## Design decisions

- **Downloads in the hosted page** use the Artifact `downloads` capability (explicit viewer confirmation). The standalone
  HTML uses a normal download. Copying the paste-prompt works in both and is the primary action.
- **The web app cannot fetch share links** because of browser cross-origin rules. It says so plainly and offers the two paths that do work:
  saving the page as HTML, or copying a one-line CLI command. No CORS proxy is used, which would mean a third party sees the chat.
- **Example-first.** The page opens on the real cricket share, converted live in the browser and clearly labelled "Example",
  so the first view shows what the product does.

# Journal 04: Dogfood and handover

**Window:** 2026-10-11 18:15 to 18:25 UTC

## Dogfood: Baton exports the session that built Baton

```bash
node src/bin.ts session latest -o examples/this-build-session
```

This turns the Claude Code session log (`~/.claude/projects/-home-user-App/<session>.jsonl`) into a bundle in the repo:
every user prompt verbatim, every assistant message, every tool call (web searches, file writes, test runs) with its output,
and the repo's source files **recovered from the session's own Write/Edit calls**. It is the "all reasoning, prompts,
outputs … saved … on GitHub" requirement, produced by the product itself.

What the export shows about Claude Code as a *source*:
- Thinking blocks are stored as signatures only, with no plaintext. The loss audit reports this (`reasoning-depth`), and the
  reasoning appears instead in the visible messages, these journals and the ADRs.
- Harness `<system-reminder>` blocks (which carry account context) are stripped and counted, not exported.
- Files edited with Python in-place scripts are reported as **stale**. This is correct: the log does not contain their final bytes.
  The committed source in `src/` is authoritative.

## Verified install paths

| Path | Result |
|---|---|
| `npx -y github:nimb-ou/App#claude/laughing-davinci-c048d8 --version` from an empty directory | `0.1.0`, then `inspect` works on the fixture |
| `claude plugin validate .` (marketplace) and on the plugin manifest | passed |
| Web app in headless Chromium, 1280 px light / 400 px dark | renders, converts the example, 0 console errors, no horizontal scroll |
| Hosted page | https://claude.ai/artifact/LNWKhj92JwA6wVtBkBMmRK (private to the owner until shared) |

## Not done / open

- **No `main` branch exists** on `nimb-ou/App`. Its only branch is this one, so a pull request has no base to target.
  Creating `main` (from this branch, or empty) is the owner's call.
- Live posting to Salesforce, Jira, Zendesk and Slack was not exercised (no credentials here). Payload shapes are unit-tested only.
- Logged-in ChatGPT chats (not shared) need the browser extension on the roadmap.
- The Stumping Recovery Lab itself (the cricket research app from the original ChatGPT thread) was **not** rebuilt. The
  user re-scoped to the transfer problem. Its handoff bundle (`examples/cricket-stumping/`) holds the 13 recovered files and a
  list of the 16 lost ones, ready for a follow-up session to continue it with `/baton:import`.

{"number":1,"title":"Build Baton handoff MVP","body":"## Summary

Builds the first usable Baton MVP: a local-first handoff for AI conversations that preserves the source, makes omissions explicit, and reconstructs files when visible code allows it.

## Included

- Shared parser for ChatGPT share HTML and exports, Claude export JSON, Claude Code JSONL, Markdown, and text.
- Node CLI that imports local files or public URLs and writes a folder or ZIP.
- Static browser app that parses locally and downloads a handoff ZIP.
- Stdio MCP server with `baton_import`, receiving-agent Skill, and draft payload builders for Salesforce, Jira, Zendesk, and Slack.
- Versioned bundle-format note, manifest hashes, privacy/limitations documentation, and build journal.

## Validation

- Node syntax checks and `git diff --check` succeeded.
- Dogfooded the importer on the repository's supplied ChatGPT share fixture: 383 visible messages, 6 audit findings, and 8 reconstructed files. The audit calls out 163 redacted tool outputs, 33 blank function inputs, and 18 sandbox links.

## Known limits

- The public share parser follows an undocumented format; original source is retained for reprocessing.
- The browser UI imports HTML/JSON/text files; direct share URL fetching is available from the CLI.

Write actions through custom MCP connectors in ChatGPT are in beta and limited to paid workspace plans. Sources differ on some details, so check OpenAI's current help article before relying on them.

- **Transports and auth:** ChatGPT supports both SSE (Server-Sent Events) and Streamable HTTP MCP transports. It supports OAuth, No Authentication, and Mixed Authentication.
- **Publishing limits:** OpenAI says apps cannot be updated after publishing at launch. To change tools or metadata after publishing, you must recreate and republish.

# 07: Capture surfaces: where Baton can live inside an AI, and what each position sees

*2026-10-11. Platform facts from vendor help pages, plus first-hand findings from v0.1.*

## The four positions

| Position | How Baton gets in | Who sees what | Platforms |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. In the page** (browser extension) | Content script in the user's logged-in tab, plus a main-world tap on `fetch` | Everything the web app itself receives: full conversation JSON including **tool outputs**, **generated files** (download endpoints), uploads, streamed tokens, branches | chatgpt.com, claude.ai, gemini.google.com (DOM), any chat site via a generic DOM adapter |
| **B. In the model's toolbox** (remote MCP relay) | Added once as a connector, after which the model calls `baton_checkpoint` / `baton_pickup` | What the **model** holds in context: decisions, plan, the latest file contents, tool results it read, its own summary. A share link never contains this. | ChatGPT developer mode (Streamable HTTP or SSE; no-auth or OAuth; write actions confirmed by the user) ([OpenAI](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12584461-developer-mode-and-mcp-apps-in-chatgpt), [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2025/10/chat-gpt-mcp)). claude.ai and Claude Desktop custom connectors (remote MCP, authless or OAuth, Free plan limited to one) ([Anthropic](https://support.anthropic.com/en/articles/11503834-building-custom-connectors-via-remote-mcp-servers)) |
| **C. In the agent's runtime** (local MCP + hooks) | stdio MCP server, plus lifecycle hooks (`PreCompact`, `SessionEnd`) that receive `transcript_path` | The **complete local log**, captured automatically **before compaction discards it** | Claude Code (plugin `hooks/hooks.json`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`) ([docs](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/hooks)), Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI (MCP) |
| **D. After the fact** (v0.1) | Share link / export / log file | Whatever the vendor published | all |

## What each position captures (ChatGPT case, from the cricket fixture)

| Item | Share link (D) | Official export (D) | Extension (A) | MCP relay (B) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| User prompts | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (model restates them) |
| Final replies | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | summary |
| Reasoning | summaries | summaries | summaries | the model's own stated rationale |
| Executed code (container.exec) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | on request |
| `functions.exec` code | ❌ blank (33) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Tool **outputs** | ❌ redacted (163) | ✅ | ✅ | the parts the model saw |
| Generated **files** (PDF, ZIP, app.py) | ❌ dead `sandbox:` links (16) | ❌ | ✅ via the download endpoint while the sandbox is alive | ✅ text files the model can reproduce |
| Content lost to context compaction | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ checkpoint taken before it is lost |
| Works with no login on the receiving side | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ (pickup code) | ✅ (pickup code) |

**Conclusion:** no single position is enough. A (extension) captures what the vendor *has*. B (MCP) captures what the
*model knows*, including in vendors where no extension can run (mobile, desktop apps, IDEs). C (hooks) makes capture automatic and
lossless for agents. Baton must unify all of them into one format and one relay.

## Transfer modes ("from within")

1. **Tab-to-tab, no server:** the extension captures in the ChatGPT tab, opens claude.ai, and injects the paste-prompt
   and attaches `HANDOFF.md` plus the recovered files to the composer. Everything stays in the browser.
2. **Pickup code via relay:** any surface sends to the relay and gets a code like `BTN-7F3K-9QXA`. Any other surface
   (MCP `baton_pickup`, the extension, `baton pickup` in a terminal, or a browser at `/h/<code>`) receives the full bundle.
3. **Shared local store:** the local stdio MCP servers in Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex and Claude Code all read and write
   `~/.baton/store`, so a handoff between two AIs on the same machine needs no server at all.

## Constraints that shape the design

- ChatGPT and claude.ai connectors call **from the vendor's cloud**, so the relay must be publicly reachable over HTTPS.
  That is a deployment step for the owner. The build ships a server, a Dockerfile and setup steps.
- The extension uses **undocumented internal endpoints** (as every exporter does). Adapters must be isolated, fail soft to DOM
  capture, and be easy to update.
- The relay stores **work content**, so: unguessable capability codes, TTL expiry (default 7 days), optional bearer token for
  private hubs, and **end-to-end encryption for extension uploads** (AES-GCM key kept in the URL fragment, never sent to the server).
  MCP uploads cannot be E2E (the model sends plaintext), which is the reason the relay is easy to self-host.

# ADR-002: Capture from within: Baton as the context bus between AIs

- **Status:** Accepted, 2026-10-11 (supersedes the "file in, file out" framing of ADR-001; ADR-001's core stays)
- **Trigger:** [prompt 004](../prompts/004-capture-from-within.md)

## Decision

Baton moves from a converter to a **relay embedded in every AI**, with three capture positions that share one bundle format
(`baton.bundle/v1`, extended with binary artifacts) and one transfer fabric.

```
           ┌────────────── capture from within ──────────────┐
 web chats │ A. Browser extension (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, …)│── tab-to-tab inject ──▶ any web chat
           │    full JSON + tool outputs + generated files    │
 any model │ B. Remote MCP relay: baton_checkpoint/pickup     │── pickup code ───────▶ any MCP client
 agents    │ C. Local MCP + hooks (PreCompact, SessionEnd)    │── ~/.baton/store ────▶ any local agent
           └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                                  ▼
                 Relay hub (self-hostable): store · /h/<code> viewer · REST · MCP
                                  ▼
                 Sinks: Salesforce · Jira · Zendesk · Slack (ADR-001)
```

## Components (this iteration)

| Component | Path | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Relay store | `src/relay/store.ts` | File-backed and versioned. Each checkpoint is hash-chained, with codes `BTN-XXXX-XXXX`, TTL and size caps. |
| Relay server | `src/relay/server.ts`, `baton relay` | MCP over Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`, REST at `/api/handoffs`, viewer at `/h/<code>`, zip at `/h/<code>.zip`. Zero dependencies. |
| Relay MCP tools | `src/relay/tools.ts` | `baton_checkpoint`, `baton_send`, `baton_pickup`, `baton_get_file`, `baton_list`. Shared by the remote server and the local stdio server. |
| Browser extension | `extension/` | MV3. Adapters for ChatGPT (backend conversation JSON + sandbox file downloads), Claude (org conversation JSON + artifacts and files), Gemini and other sites (DOM). In-page panel: capture, save zip, copy prompt, **Continue in…** (tab-to-tab injection), **Send to relay**. |
| Claude Code hooks | `hooks/hooks.json`, `baton hook` | Auto-bundle on `PreCompact` and `SessionEnd` into `.baton/sessions/`. |
| Pickup CLI | `baton pickup <code>`, `baton send <bundle>` | For terminals. |

## Format change: binary artifacts

`BatonArtifact.encoding?: 'utf8' | 'base64'`. Captured PDFs, images and ZIPs ship as bytes under `files/`. The hash is over the decoded bytes.
New artifact status: none. Captured files are `recovered`, with `note: "captured from source"`.

## Alternatives rejected

- **Scraping the DOM everywhere.** It misses tool outputs and files. Used only as a fallback.
- **A hosted-only SaaS relay.** Vendor connectors need a public URL, so hosting is offered, but the relay must stay self-hostable for trust.
- **Bundling a cloud LLM to summarise.** The model doing the work writes the checkpoint. That is better context at zero inference cost.

## Risks

- Internal web endpoints change. Adapters are small, versioned and fall back to DOM capture. Tests run against recorded fixtures.
- Relay data sensitivity. Mitigated by TTL, codes, bearer token, E2E for extension uploads, and redaction on by default.

args.content:
# Embedding Baton in every AI

Baton works from **inside** each assistant, so it captures what share links and exports drop (tool outputs, generated
files, the model's own state) and moves it to another assistant without downloading or uploading files.

```
 ChatGPT ──┐                                               ┌── ChatGPT
 Claude  ──┤  in-page extension  ──── tab-to-tab ─────────▶├── Claude
 Gemini  ──┤                                               ├── Gemini
 any AI  ──┤  MCP: baton_checkpoint ─▶ relay ─▶ baton_pickup├── any AI with the connector
 agents  ──┘  hooks / local MCP ─────▶ ~/.baton/store ─────└── any local agent
```

## 1. Browser extension (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini on the web)

1. `npm run build` (or use the committed `extension/dist/`).
2. Chrome / Edge / Brave → `chrome://extensions` → Developer mode → **Load unpacked** → choose `extension/dist`.
3. Open a conversation and click **Baton** (bottom right) → **Capture this conversation**.

| Site | How it captures | What it gets that a share link does not |
|---|---|---|
| ChatGPT | The page's own conversation API with your session, plus each `sandbox:/mnt/data/…` file through the download endpoint, plus your uploads | Every tool output, `functions.exec` code, generated files (PDF, ZIP, code) **as bytes**, uploads. Capture before the sandbox expires. |
| Claude | The page's full conversation API (`render_all_tools`) | Tool calls and results, thinking, artifacts (create/update replayed into files), `create_file` outputs |
| Gemini | Rendered page plus the raw response stream observed while generating | Visible turns and code. The raw stream is kept under `files/live-streams/`. |

Then use **Copy prompt**, **Save .zip**, **Continue in → Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini** (opens the other AI, fills its
message box and attaches `HANDOFF.md` plus the files; you press send), or **Send to relay** (end-to-end encrypted by default).

Permissions: the four chat sites, the ChatGPT file host, and (only if you set one) your relay's origin.
Nothing is sent anywhere unless you click Send.

## 2. MCP: let the model checkpoint and pick up work itself

The model calls `baton_checkpoint` with what it holds in context: full file contents, tool outputs, verbatim prompts, decisions and next steps.
It returns a pickup code. In any other AI, `baton_pickup <code>` returns the handoff brief plus the files.

### Web assistants need a reachable relay

```bash
npx github:nimb-ou/App relay --port 8787            # or: docker build -t baton-relay . && docker run -p 8787:8787 baton-relay
# expose it over HTTPS (any reverse proxy, Render via render.yaml, Fly, Cloud Run…) and set BATON_PUBLIC_URL
```

| Assistant | Where to add it |
|---|---|
| **ChatGPT** | Settings → Apps & Connectors → Advanced → **Developer mode** → Create → URL `https://<relay>/mcp` (or `/mcp/<BATON_MCP_SECRET>`), auth "No authentication". Write tools (checkpoint) require a plan with developer-mode write actions. Read-only plans can still **pick up**. |
| **Claude** (web, desktop) | Settings → Connectors → **Add custom connector** → `https://<relay>/mcp` |
| **Claude Code** | `claude mcp add --transport http baton https://<relay>/mcp`, or install the plugin (local, below) |
| **Cursor / Codex / Gemini CLI / others** | Add an HTTP MCP server with the same URL |

Use it by saying *"baton: hand this off"*, then in the other assistant *"baton pickup BTN-7F3K-9QXA-2M4P"*.
The relay also serves `https://<relay>/h/<code>` (viewer) and `/h/<code>.zip`.

Relay settings: `BATON_PUBLIC_URL`, `BATON_MCP_SECRET` (serve MCP only at `/mcp/<secret>`), `BATON_RELAY_TOKEN`
(bearer for REST uploads), `BATON_TTL_DAYS` (default 7), `BATON_MAX_BYTES` (default 25 MB), `BATON_STORE`.

### Local agents need no server

Any stdio MCP client can run `npx -y github:nimb-ou/App mcp`. Every local agent then shares `~/.baton/store`, so
Claude Desktop → Cursor → Claude Code handoffs work offline. Set `BATON_RELAY_URL` to point them at a hub instead.

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "baton": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "github:nimb-ou/App", "mcp"] } } }
```

## 3. Claude Code plugin: automatic capture

`/plugin marketplace add nimb-ou/App` → `/plugin install baton@baton` gives you:
- the **baton** skill, plus `/baton:import` and `/baton:handoff`
- the MCP server (file tools plus checkpoint and pickup)
- **hooks**: on `PreCompact` and `SessionEnd`, the full transcript is bundled into `.baton/sessions/<time>-<event>-<id>/`
  **before compaction discards it**. Set `BATON_AUTO_SEND=1` and `BATON_RELAY_URL` to also send each snapshot.

## 4. Terminal

```bash
baton send handoffs/my-work --relay https://<relay> --seal   # → https://<relay>/h/BTN-…#key
baton pickup "https://<relay>/h/BTN-…#key"                  # → handoffs/BTN-…/HANDOFF.md
```

## Security model

- Pickup codes are 60-bit capability tokens, so treat them like a link to a private doc. Handoffs expire (7 days by default).
- **Sealed** uploads (extension and CLI `--seal`) are AES-GCM encrypted in the sender's browser or terminal. The key exists only
  in the link's `#fragment`, which browsers never send to servers. The relay stores ciphertext only.
- MCP checkpoints cannot be sealed, because the model sends plaintext to the server. Self-host the relay, or use the local store.
- Redaction (keys, tokens, emails, phones) runs before anything leaves the capture point.

**Hand off AI work, not just chat text.**

Baton turns an AI conversation into a **handoff bundle** that another tool, agent, teammate or business system can pick up and continue.
